newsitem.title: USA: No. American 1996 platinum demand seen down - JM.
newsitem.headline: No. American 1996 platinum demand seen down - JM.

text.p: North American demand for platinum for use in autocatalysts, used to control pollution, is forecast to decline about three percent this year, refiner Johnson Matthey said in its 1996 interim review published Tuesday.
But palladium demand is seen jumping about 31 percent as automakers continue to switch from platinum to palladium-based emission control devices, the report said.

North American platinum demand is forecast to slip 25,000 ounces to 765,000 ounces in 1996 from 790,000 ounces in 1995, while palladium demand is seen rising to 1,165,000 ounces in 1996 from 885,000 in 1995, Johnson Matthey said.

"This decline is principally due to changes in catalyst fitment by the Ford Motor Company, which is equipping an increasing proportion of its fleet with palladium-rich and palladium-only catalysts," the report said.
"Overall platinum consumption by other manufacturers has remained stable," Johnson Matthey marketing manager Jeremey Coombes said.
North America is the largest user of both platinum and palladium of any region in the world.

World platinum demand is seen slipping to 1,820,000 ounces this year from 1,850,000 ounces last year, while world palladium demand is forecast to jump to 2,270,000 ounces this year from 1,730,000 ounces last year.
The platinum supply/demand balance in 1996 is seen tightening in 1996, with the world surplus reducing to 80,000 ounces from 190,000 ounces last year, Johnson Matthey said.
Autocatalysts account for about 38 percent of world platinum demand.
Average loadings on platinum-rich auto catalysts in North America will be little changed this year, since there has been no further tightening of U.S. federal emissions controls, the report said.
The phase-in of stricter limits under the U.S. Clean Air Act 1990 was complete by end of 1995, the report noted.

But, in the first eight months of 1996, last year's 2.5 percent fall in light vehicle sales in the U.S. was reversed, and auto registrations are expected to expand by three pct in 1996 as a whole, with growth concentrated in the light truck center.
"Most U.S. automakers will consume more palladium in the next few years as larger numbers of Low Emission Vehicles (LEV) are manufactured to comply with legislation in California," the report said.

In 1996 Massachusetts and New York adopted new emissions limits based on the California model, and the adoption of a national LEV programme is under discussion between automakers, state legislators and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
A decision is expected late this year and the new limits are likely to be phased in between 1997 and 2001, encouraging further growth in palladium demand, Johnson Matthey said.

Demand for palladium from the North American petroleum refining industry will also be strong, with further purchases likely of a platinum-palladium catalyst used to reduce the aromatics content of diesel fuel.
Among other platinum group metals, there were substantial purchases of ruthenium for new ammonia plants operating the Kellogg Advanced Ammonia Process, the report said.
Facilities using this process are now in operation in North America, and new capacity is under construction in Trinidad, where natural gas (the main feedstock for ammonia production) is abundant.
During 1996 there were also purchases of an iridium-based catalyst used in a new process for the production of acetic acid.
This catalyst is already in use in the USA and will be installed in plants in Europe and Asia in 1997 and 1998.
